content: 1. It is essential to address people's health needs while respecting their rights and responsibilities regarding their own health. This includes engaging stakeholders in the development and implementation of health policies. 2. Coordination of health services within the health sector and fostering intersectoral collaboration is critical to addressing the broader social determinants of health. A holistic approach to health services should encompass health promotion, disease prevention, diagnosis, treatment, disease management, rehabilitation, and palliative care. 3. Where appropriate, traditional and complementary medicine should be integrated into health services, based on national contexts and evidence-based policies. This integration must ensure the safety, quality, and effectiveness of health services while maintaining a holistic approach to health. 4. International, regional, and national partners are encouraged to take note of the framework for integrated, people-centered health services. 5. The Director-General is requested to provide technical support and guidance to Member States for implementing, adapting, and operationalizing the framework for integrated, people-centered health services, with a focus on strengthening primary health services. 6. The Director-General should ensure alignment and active engagement across all levels of the organization in promoting and implementing the framework for integrated, people-centered health services. 7. Research and development of indicators to monitor global progress on integrated, people-centered health services should be conducted. 8. Progress on the implementation of the framework for integrated, people-centered health services should be reported to the World Health Assembly at regular intervals. 9. Palliative care is a critical approach to improving the quality of life for patients and their families facing life-threatening illnesses. It involves the prevention and relief of suffering through early identification, assessment, and treatment of pain and other physical, psychosocial, or spiritual problems. 10. Palliative care is fundamental to enhancing quality of life, well-being, comfort, and human dignity. It is a person-centered health service that values patients' need for adequate, culturally sensitive information about their health status and their central role in treatment decisions. 11. Access to palliative care and essential medicines, including opioid analgesics like morphine, is a key component of the right to the highest attainable standard of health and well-being. 12. Health systems have an ethical responsibility to provide palliative care, and healthcare professionals have a duty to alleviate pain and suffering, regardless of whether the underlying disease can be cured. End-of-life care is a critical component of palliative care. 13. More than 40 million people require palliative care annually, and this need is expected to grow with aging populations and the rise of chronic diseases. Palliative care is particularly important for children, and Member States should estimate the quantities of controlled medicines needed, including pediatric formulations. 14. Palliative care must be integrated across the continuum of care, especially at the primary care level. Inadequate integration of palliative care into health and social care systems contributes to inequitable access to such care. 15. The availability and appropriate use of internationally controlled medicines for medical and scientific purposes, particularly for pain and symptom relief, remain insufficient in many countries. Efforts to prevent the diversion of controlled substances should not create regulatory barriers to medical access. 16. Education and training for healthcare providers and caregivers, including family members and non-governmental organization workers, are essential to address the lack of knowledge about palliative care. 17. Palliative care employs an interdisciplinary approach to address the needs of patients and their families. Strong networks between professional palliative care providers, support care providers, volunteers, and affected families are crucial for delivering quality care. 18. Palliative care is needed across all disease groups, including noncommunicable and infectious diseases, and for all age groups. 19. Palliative care should be included in the definition of universal health coverage, and health services must provide integrated palliative care equitably to meet patients' needs. 20. Adequate funding mechanisms for palliative care programs, including medicines and medical products, are necessary, particularly in developing countries. 21. The inclusion of palliative care actions and indicators in WHO's global monitoring framework for noncommunicable diseases and the global action plan for their prevention and control is commendable. 22. Medicines for pain and symptom control in palliative care settings are included in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, and efforts to improve access to palliative care are recognized. 23. Governments and civil society should collaborate to support the provision of palliative care services, including the availability and appropriate use of controlled substances for medical purposes. 24. Member States are urged to develop and implement palliative care policies to strengthen health systems and integrate evidence-based, cost-effective, and equitable palliative care services across all levels of care, with an emphasis on primary, community, and home-based care. 25. Domestic funding and human resources should be allocated for palliative care initiatives, including policy development, education, training, and quality improvement. 26. Basic training and continuing education on palliative care should be integrated into undergraduate medical and nursing education and in-service training for primary care providers. 27. Intermediate training should be offered to healthcare workers who routinely care for patients with life-threatening illnesses, including those in oncology, infectious diseases, pediatrics, geriatrics, and internal medicine. 28. Specialist palliative care training should be available to prepare healthcare professionals to manage complex symptom management needs. 29. Domestic palliative care needs, including pain management medication requirements, should be assessed, and collaborative action should ensure an adequate supply of essential medicines. 30. National and local legislation and policies for controlled medicines should be reviewed and revised, where appropriate, to improve access to pain management medicines in line with WHO guidance and international drug control conventions. 31. National essential medicines lists should be updated to include pain and palliative care medicines as outlined in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines. 32. Partnerships between governments and civil society, including patient organizations, should be fostered to support palliative care services. 33. Palliative care actions included in WHO's global action plan for noncommunicable diseases should be implemented and monitored. 34. The Director-General is requested to ensure that palliative care is integrated into all relevant global disease control and health system plans, including those related to noncommunicable diseases and universal health coverage. 35. Evidence-based guidelines and tools on palliative care, including pain management options for adults and children, should be developed and disseminated. 36. National health systems should integrate palliative care across disease groups and levels of care, addressing ethical issues such as equitable access, person-centered care, and community involvement. 37. WHO should support Member States in reviewing and improving national legislation and policies to balance the prevention of misuse and diversion of controlled substances with appropriate access to controlled medicines. 38. Efforts should be made to increase the availability and accessibility of medicines used in palliative care through consultation with Member States, networks, civil society, and international stakeholders. 39. WHO should collaborate with the International Narcotics Control Board, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, and health ministries to promote the availability and balanced control of controlled medicines for pain and symptom management. 40. Accurate estimates of controlled medicines needed for pain relief and palliative care should be established to ensure their availability.
